stories.title_en: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings

comments.author: enthuseyourcurb
comments.text:
As someone working at a bigtech co that has spent every single working day (and many weekends) since the launch of Mythos patching serious, company-ending type of security issues, these types of posts really irk me.
Public datasets of CVEs being underwhelming doesn't mean much if all of the issues are in private company codebases that will never get a CVE number assigned and will never get a fancy blog post. You're never going to hear about them, and the people working on them probably can't tell you about them, but that doesn't mean they don't exist.
We're all worried about OSS having security issues because of how widely used things like PHP or curl are... but the same can be said about email providers, document collaboration SaaSes, payment processors, etc that millions of companies depend. Those companies will never be in datasets like this, and they'll never publicly disclose how many issues they found.

comments.author: pizlonator
comments.text:
I received 9 reports of Fil-C issues from Anthropic
All of them were real bugs. None of them were false positives.
The quality of the reports was exceptional. (My baseline is doing security defense on a browser engine, so my baseline has a large sample count and is probably representative of what experts are capable of.)
The quality of the proposed fixes was alright. I took some of the fixes verbatim. I used most of the fixes as significant inspiration for doing it my way.
The quality of the test cases was exceptional.
Maybe I’m special somehow! But I just want to call out the enormous chasm between what I saw of anthropic’s capability and what TFA says

comments.author: snowwrestler
comments.text:
The PHP2Shell vulnerability ended up being paradoxically comforting for me.
They turned frontier models loose on PHP, and the big one they found was based on a previously known logic flaw that was extremely difficult to exploit. Which makes sense: hence the need for frontier models.
And in the wild, while there have been many attempts and a few simple demo successes, the practical impact has seemed to be small, seemingly constrained by the length of the chain and the diversity of PHP configs.
In short, it was indeed a major vulnerability, but not magic (in the Arthur C Clarke sense).
I think ultimately the fear comes down to: do you believe that code can be secured. I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc. But if one believes code can be constructed to operate to spec, then there must be a limit to the damage an LLM can do, even a very smart one.
I think we are going through a phase where a lot of known triaged code shortcomings will get exposed and hopefully fixed. Sucks while it is happening. But not actually the first round of this type of evolution. And ultimately I think as before, we will come out the othe

Isn't the whole point of glasswing to patch stuff way before it can be exploited? If the patched code is distributed quickly- there's no opportunity (or incentive) for bad actors to craft and distribute an exploit. This reads like an attempt to spin them as not being "real" vulnerabilities.

comments.author: rurcliped
comments.text:
The blog is misleading because it tries to characterize Project Glasswing's effectiveness through use of a tangentially related data source. A Project Glasswing vulnerability discovery most often occurs when a Glasswing partner points a Mythos-class model at its own, often proprietary, software. The data source (aka "ledger") is only for the Anthropic coordinated vulnerability disclosure program for open source software: in other words, Anthropic itself pointing a Mythos-class model at an OSS package, and then notifying the maintainer afterward that it had done this, and had findings to share. This OSS work is certainly useful, but the number of fixes reflects - in part - limited time availability by volunteer OSS maintainers, and Anthropic sometimes working without knowledge of the OSS project's threat model (the threat model is explicitly requested in the newer oss-scanner effort). Percentage fixed is often much higher for use of Glasswing with proprietary software, e.g.,
https://blog.cloudflare.com/cyber-frontier-models/

comments.author: arlattimore
comments.text: The post seems misguided or misdirected in my opinion. Not discounting the fact that the frontier models may find existing bugs, that some are labelled at the incorrect level, even some being a non-bug -- fact remains they are discovering vast numbers of issues. It also isn't the job of Anthropic or OpenAI to fix everyone's bugs, they are doing everyone a courtesy to spend their time identifying them in the first place. The bigger issue appears to be that they are finding more bugs than the developer capacity to can address.

comments.author: delichon
comments.text: It is bad if this points to a general pattern of AI being better at finding than fixing vulnerabilities. The larger that ratio, the harder to secure all the things. The current stat from this experiment is 37,966 to 217. Lots of false positives, but not enough to change the big picture. I hope they didn't apply equivalent tokens to both sides, or AI may be better at demolition than construction.

stories.title_en: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America

comments.author: freetime2
comments.text:
I use a kei truck for farming. They are incredibly pragmatic little vehicles. They are very capable driving around on dirt/gravel agricultural roads with 4WD, and they are inexpensive and robust enough that you can really beat them up and use them as a tool without worry. Repairs and replacement parts are ubiquitous and inexpensive. Having the
sides
of bed fold down is also really useful.
They aren't comfortable to drive at all (although just having A/C at all on a hot summer day in the field is a godsend), and I wouldn't want to do longer trips in one - although you certainly could in a pinch.
It seems like Toyota/Scion is just testing the waters here, and I'm not sure how successful they'll be. But I hope there is a future for kei trucks in the US.

comments.author: ilamont
comments.text:
25 mph works for golf courses, resort, or island use. In rural areas on the mainland, roads connecting towns often have 45 or 55 mph speed limits so unless you plan on staying on the farm I don't think these are practical for trips to go shopping, dumping, hauling, etc.
As for the imports, I saw one of these 90s-era right-hand drive kei trucks at a parking lot a few months ago and talked with the owner. He was a young guy who lived in Boston, said it was super easy to park. Speed maxed out at 70 mph, which is fine for local trips but maybe not for long highway trips.
For people in jurisdictions that allow 30 year old truck imports, and are interested in getting one, there are other countries that use such trucks and have left-hand drive. Taiwan has models from CMC and Suzuki, and I believe South Korea also makes them.

I had a good use for it at the time (a family move) so I regret not getting it, since I figured it would just be more lingering crap at the end of the move.  But, it would have held resale value. comments.author: iainctduncan
comments.text:
People here might be interested to know that you can run Scheme (lisp) code directly in Ableton through my Scheme for Max project in Max for Live.
S4M is an open source extension to Max that allows you to run the s7 Scheme interpreter in a Max object, similar to the JS object in Max. Advantages over JS are that in can run in the high priority scheduler thread, enabling accurate timing, it has direct access to the file system from Scheme code, and allows you to make Scheme s-expressions directly in Max messages. It is also a very nice way to control the Live API, as the live API works on lists of symbols.
https://github.com/iainctduncan/scheme-for-max
https://www.youtube.com/c/musicwithlisp
I'm planning another major release in the next few months as part of my PhD work.

I'm not sure that "AI generates..." articles are going to age well.
My immediate question would be what kind of adversarial reviews and deterministic gates did the author write to capture the dimensions of maintainability (lack of DRY, cyclomatic complexity, unclear naming, poorly architected flows, etc) that they cared about.
Don't get me wrong. When I was speeding along at 200 PRs a day (personal projects - I would not have inflicted them on others) I pretty quickly slopped together a big ball of mud, but as I'm re-generating my estate (a) the models are a little better but (b) I'm adding a lot more rigor around verification (correctness, performance, security, operational costs and maintainability). It's not an easy problem to solve, but it feels to me like an engineering endeavor, not speculative rocket science.
I fully understand that many AI generated code bases do indeed suffer from more incidents and less maintainability, but I think it's important to distinguish between what is common and what is possible as the fix for one is improving the rigor of your verification whereas the fix for the other would be either accepting crappy code or giving up on LLMs.

comments.author: jasode
comments.text:
I don't disagree with the article but it may give some readers the impression that pre-AI hand-written code wasn't fragile.
Here's the famous commentary about Oracle RDBMS codebase of 25 million lines:
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18442941
Every big company codebase with millions of lines devolves into a similar state.  The small codebase starts with clean conceptual integrity.  It then inevitably decays into incomprehensible spaghetti code as more people are added to it.  Various reasons for it including the later devs caring less about the code than the initial team of devs, deadlines, avoiding refactoring because of fear about breaking things, etc.
If you don't want AI to create fragile code, you have to apply the same quality gates that would have been applied to pre-AI hand-written code to keep everything clean.  Most companies don't do that.

Not sure why you'd vibe-code a new VPN protocol, double ratchet or otherwise, when you can just take WireGuard and make a new transport for it.
WireGuard by itself is not a stealth VPN, but the things that make a VPN "stealthy" are all things you'd layer on top of a WireGuard design, not thread through the middle of it. A datagram-based protocol can run under any obscured transport.
We did this at Fly.io when we discovered that, for one reason or another, 5% of our users simply couldn't reliably use UDP. It was a one-day project to run it under WebSockets instead, and that was before coding agents.
